questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — spread.

options.misconception: Assuming the spread discards the extra value
Counting the spread as adding two values

questions.explanation: The spread expands the two existing entries and the trailing value is appended, giving 3 elements. The spread form creates a fresh array rather than mutating arr. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming the spread discards the extra value, counting the spread as adding two values and reporting only the appended element.
questions.hint: Spread copies existing items before the new one is added.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — hoisting.
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies, so typeof reports 'function' even before the source line. Their value is available throughout the enclosing scope. The printed value is function, while the alternatives come from assuming declarations are not hoisted, expecting the return value instead and thinking the early reference throws.
questions.hint: Declarations, unlike expressions, are initialized during hoisting.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — closures.

options.misconception: Assuming the closure resets each call

questions.explanation: The closure keeps n alive between calls; the first invocation raises it to 3098 and the second to 3099. Each call mutates the same captured binding. The printed value is 3099, while the alternatives come from counting only the first increment, assuming the closure resets each call and counting three increments.
questions.hint: A closure retains the variable, it does not copy it per call.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — defaults.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 3099.

options.misconception: Assuming a missing argument becomes zero
Thinking defaults do not apply to calls

questions.explanation: A default parameter is used when the argument is omitted, so label returns 3099. Passing undefined explicitly would also trigger the default. The printed value is 3099, while the alternatives come from assuming a missing argument becomes zero, thinking defaults do not apply to calls and adding one to the default.
questions.hint: Defaults apply when an argument is missing or undefined.
